description: Occurs when you attempt to use an object reference that has not been initialized (points to null). Java throws this unchecked runtime exception when calling methods or accessing fields on a null object.
common_causes: Calling a method on an uninitialized object
Accessing an array element that is null
Method returning null that caller doesn't check
fix: Always initialize objects before use. Use Optional<T> or null checks. Leverage @NonNull annotations, Objects.requireNonNull(), or the Null Object Pattern.
code_example:
String s = null;
System.out.println(s.length()); // NullPointerException

description: Thrown when you attempt to access an array with an index that is either negative or greater than or equal to the size of the array.
common_causes: Off-by-one error in loop condition (using <= instead of <)
Hardcoded index that doesn't match array size
fix: Always validate that the index is within bounds (0 to array.length - 1). Prefer enhanced for-loops or iterators when index is not needed.
code_example:
int[] arr = {1, 2, 3};
System.out.println(arr[3]); // ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException

description: Occurs when the call stack overflows due to infinite or excessively deep recursion. Each method call consumes stack space; without a proper base case, the stack fills up.
common_causes: Base case that is never reached
fix: Ensure every recursive function has a clearly reachable base case. Consider converting deep recursion to iterative approach using an explicit Stack data structure.
practice_problems: LeetCode 104 - Maximum Depth of Binary Tree

description: Thrown when you attempt to cast an object to a class that it is not an instance of. Common when working with raw types or collections without generics.
fix: Use instanceof before casting. Use generics to enforce type safety at compile time. Use pattern matching instanceof in Java 16+.
code_example:
Object obj = "Hello";
Integer i = (Integer) obj; // ClassCastException

description: Raised when a dictionary key is not found in the dictionary. Python raises this when using square bracket notation to access a key that doesn't exist.
common_causes: Accessing a key that was never added to the dict
fix: Use dict.get(key, default) for safe access. Use defaultdict for automatic default values. Check key existence with 'in' operator before access.
code_example:
data = {'name': 'Alice'}
print(data['age'])  # KeyError: 'age'

description: Raised when an attribute reference or assignment fails. Common when calling a method on None or accessing an attribute that doesn't exist on an object.
common_causes: Calling method on None (function returned None implicitly)
Accessing class-level attribute as instance or vice versa
fix: Check if the object is None before accessing attributes. Verify method names via dir(obj). Use hasattr(obj, 'attr') for conditional access.
code_example:
result = some_function()  # Returns None
result.do_something()  # AttributeError: 'NoneType'
fix_code:
result = some_function()
if result is not None:
    result.do_something()
# Or using getattr safely:
getattr(result, 'do_something', lambda: None)()
practice_problems: LeetCode 237 - Delete Node in Linked List

description: Raised when a sequence subscript is out of range. Similar to Java's ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException but for Python lists, tuples, and strings.
fix: Validate list length before indexing. Use try/except IndexError. Use list slicing which is forgiving with out-of-bound indices.
code_example:
lst = [1, 2, 3]
print(lst[5])  # IndexError: list index out of range
fix_code:
lst = [1, 2, 3]
# Safe access
index = 5
if index < len(lst):
    print(lst[index])
# Or with get pattern
value = next(iter(lst[5:]), None)  # Returns None if out of bounds

description: Raised when an operation or function is applied to an object of an inappropriate type. Python is dynamically typed, making this a common runtime error.
fix: Use type hints and runtime type checking. Validate input types with isinstance(). Use explicit type conversion (str(), int(), float()).
code_example:
age = 25
message = 'Age is: ' + age  # TypeError: can only concatenate str (not 'int')
fix_code:
age = 25
message = f'Age is: {age}'  # f-string handles conversion
# Or explicitly:
message = 'Age is: ' + str(age)

description: Raised when the maximum recursion depth (default 1000 in CPython) is exceeded. Python equivalent of Java's StackOverflowError.
common_causes: Missing base case in recursive function
Deep tree/graph recursion without stack management
fix: Add proper base case. Use sys.setrecursionlimit() cautiously. Convert to iterative approach. Use @functools.lru_cache for memoization to avoid recomputation.
code_example:
def fib(n):
    return fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)  # No base case!

description: Raised when the divisor in a division or modulo operation is zero. Basic arithmetic safety violation.
fix: Always validate the denominator before division. Use try/except ZeroDivisionError. Return a sentinel value (None, 0, or float('inf')) in case of zero.
code_example:
def average(total, count):
    return total / count  # ZeroDivisionError if count == 0

error_type: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined
description: Occurs when you try to access a property or method of undefined or null in JavaScript. The JS equivalent of NullPointerException.
common_causes: Async data not yet loaded when accessed
Array out of bounds returning undefined
fix: Use optional chaining (?.) for safe property access. Use nullish coalescing (??) for fallback values. Guard with conditional checks before deep property access.
code_example:
const user = undefined;
console.log(user.name); // TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined

description: Thrown when you access a variable that hasn't been declared in the current or any enclosing scope.
common_causes: Accessing let/const before declaration (Temporal Dead Zone)
Variable declared inside a block accessed outside
fix: Declare variables with let or const before use. Understand block scoping with let/const vs function scoping with var. Check import statements for external modules.
code_example:
console.log(count); // ReferenceError
let count = 0;

description: Occurs when a Promise is rejected and no rejection handler is attached. In modern Node.js, unhandled rejections crash the process.
fix: Always add .catch() to promise chains or use try/catch with async/await. Add a global unhandledRejection handler for safety net logging.

description: React throws this error when a component triggers an update that causes another update, creating an infinite loop. Usually caused by incorrect useEffect dependencies or setState calls in render.
common_causes: Missing or incorrect dependency array in useEffect
Dependency array contains objects/functions that change every render
fix: Audit useEffect dependencies. Never call setState unconditionally in useEffect. Use useMemo/useCallback for stable references. Add condition before setState.

description: A segfault occurs when a program tries to access memory that it is not authorized to access. This is a critical low-level error that causes program termination.
common_causes: Dereferencing a null or dangling pointer
Buffer overflow / writing past array bounds
Use-after-free: accessing memory that was already freed
fix: Always initialize pointers. Check for null before dereferencing. Use smart pointers (unique_ptr, shared_ptr) in C++. Use valgrind or AddressSanitizer to detect memory errors.
code_example:
int *ptr = nullptr;
*ptr = 42; // Segmentation fault!
practice_problems: Implement a Linked List in C

description: A deadlock occurs when two or more threads or transactions are waiting for each other to release locks, creating a circular wait condition that halts all progress.
common_causes: Two transactions locking resources in opposite order
N+1 update patterns causing table-level locks
fix: Always acquire locks in the same consistent order. Use lock timeouts. Keep transactions short. Use optimistic locking (versioning) instead of pessimistic locking where possible.
code_example:
-- Transaction 1: LOCK A, then tries to lock B
-- Transaction 2: LOCK B, then tries to lock A
-- Both are stuck!
fix_code:
-- Solution 1: Consistent lock ordering
-- Always lock tables in alphabetical order

-- Solution 2: Use SELECT FOR UPDATE with SKIP LOCKED
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending'
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 10;

-- Solution 3: Optimistic locking with version column
UPDATE orders SET status='processed', version=version+1
WHERE id=1 AND version=5;

description: The N+1 problem occurs when code executes 1 query to get a list of N items, then N additional queries to fetch related data for each item — resulting in N+1 total queries and catastrophic performance.
common_causes: Lazy loading in ORMs (Hibernate, SQLAlchemy, TypeORM)
Missing JOIN or eager loading configuration
fix: Use eager loading (JOIN FETCH in JPQL, include in Sequelize, select_related in Django). Use batch fetching. Use DataLoader pattern for GraphQL.
code_example:
# Django ORM - N+1 Problem
authors = Author.objects.all()  # 1 query
for author in authors:
    print(author.books.count())  # N queries!
fix_code:
# Django - Fix with select_related / prefetch_related
authors = Author.objects.prefetch_related('books').all()  # 2 queries total
for author in authors:
    print(author.books.count())  # No extra queries!

description: Container or pod is killed by the OOM (Out Of Memory) killer because it exceeded its memory limit. Exit code 137 = SIGKILL, typically from OOM killer.
common_causes: Memory limit set too low for workload
Unbounded data processing (streaming large files into memory)
Missing resource limits in pod spec
fix: Set appropriate memory limits and requests. Fix memory leaks using profiling tools. Use streaming for large data. Monitor with metrics + alerts.
code_example:
# Pod keeps restarting with OOMKilled
# kubectl describe pod my-pod shows: OOMKilled
fix_code:
# Set proper resource limits in k8s:
resources:
  requests:
    memory: '256Mi'
  limits:
    memory: '512Mi'

# Stream large files instead of loading all into memory:
with open('large_file.csv', 'r') as f:
    for chunk in pd.read_csv(f, chunksize=1000):
        process(chunk)

description: Raised when a network connection attempt is actively refused by the target host. The server is not listening on the specified port.
common_causes: Service not started on the target port
Service crashed or not yet ready during startup
fix: Verify the service is running and listening. Check .env / config for correct host:port. Implement retry logic with exponential backoff for startup race conditions.
code_example:
import socket
s = socket.connect(('localhost', 5432))  # DB not started!

description: Thrown when a collection is modified while iterating over it using an iterator. Java's fail-fast iterators detect structural modification and throw this exception.
common_causes: Removing elements from a list inside a for-each loop
Adding elements to a collection while iterating
fix: Use Iterator.remove() instead of collection.remove(). Use CopyOnWriteArrayList for concurrent use. Collect elements to remove separately, then remove after iteration.

description: Raised when Python cannot locate the specified module. ModuleNotFoundError is a subclass of ImportError for missing modules.
common_causes: Package not installed in current virtual environment
Wrong package name (PyPI name differs from import name)
fix: Install the missing package via pip. Activate the virtual environment. Check import name vs pip install name. Restructure circular imports using lazy imports.
code_example: import numpy  # ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'numpy'
fix_code:
# 1. Install the package
# pip install numpy

# 2. Verify environment
# python -m pip list | grep numpy

# 3. For circular imports, use lazy import
def get_module():
    import heavy_module  # Imported lazily inside function
    return heavy_module

description: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) error occurs when a browser blocks a frontend web page from making requests to a different domain due to the Same-Origin Policy.
common_causes: Frontend on localhost:3000 calling API on localhost:8000 without CORS config
Credentials (cookies) sent cross-origin without explicit allow
fix: Configure CORS middleware on the backend to allow specific origins. For FastAPI, use CORSMiddleware. Never use wildcard (*) for credentialed requests.
fix_code:
# FastAPI CORS fix:
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware

app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=['http://localhost:3000', 'http://localhost:5173'],
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=['*'],
    allow_headers=['*'],
)

description: Thrown when the JVM cannot allocate an object in the heap because the heap is exhausted and garbage collection cannot free sufficient memory.
common_causes: Memory leak (objects not released, growing collections)
Loading entire large file into memory
Heap size configured too small for workload
fix: Increase heap size with -Xmx flag. Fix memory leaks using heap profiler (VisualVM, JProfiler). Use streaming APIs for large data. Analyze with GC logs.

description: A race condition occurs when the behavior of a program depends on the sequence or timing of uncontrollable events like thread execution order, leading to non-deterministic bugs.
common_causes: Multiple threads reading and writing shared state without synchronization
Check-then-act operations that are not atomic
fix: Use locks (threading.Lock in Python, synchronized in Java). Use thread-safe data structures. Use atomic operations. Prefer immutable state.
code_example:
counter = 0
def increment():
    global counter
    counter += 1  # NOT atomic! Race condition here
fix_code:
import threading

counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def increment():
    global counter
    with lock:  # Thread-safe
        counter += 1

# Or use atomic operations:
from threading import Lock
from collections import Counter
thread_safe_counter = Counter()  # Some operations are atomic in CPython

description: Raised by the Python parser when code doesn't conform to the Python language grammar. Code with a SyntaxError cannot be executed at all.
common_causes: Using Python 2 print statement in Python 3
fix: Read the error message carefully — it usually points to the exact line. Use an IDE with syntax highlighting. Check indentation consistency (spaces vs tabs).
code_example:
def greet(name)
    print(f'Hello {name}')  # SyntaxError: expected ':'
fix_code:
def greet(name):  # Added colon
    print(f'Hello {name}')

greet('World')
